title: Design of polymer configuration and flow
contribution: A group test-problem page that packages an inverse polymer-design problem (six inputs to the black-box tube-model simulator bob) with run instructions for derivative-free optimization, without a reference solution.
problem_entry: Rheology of polymer melts must be controlled for processing and is very sensitive to architecture, so the problem is inverse: find all architectures whose simulated rheology resembles a target (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Treat the extended tube model simulator bob as a black box over six inputs (mole fraction, weight-averaged mass and PDI of each component of a binary star-polymer blend), wrapped by an executable with a file interface (myin to myout) (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Tube model of polymer motion (p. 2); the objective (how resemblance is measured), bounds, budget and evaluation cost are not given in the text, and Figure 1 with the fixed parameters was not extracted (pp. 2-4).
experiments: none in this item; the experiments are said to be in Sun et al. 2020, INDEX S111, not read (pp. 2, 4)
positioning: Cites only the bob simulator papers and the group's own DFO paper (p. 4).
writing: Four-page problem page: background, the inverse-design question in one sentence, then setup and run instructions for Linux and Windows (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: No limits are stated; no reference solution, known optimum or expected number of architectures is given (pp. 1-4).

method_links.note: step 5 (publish problems): a public, runnable black-box test problem, but with no certified optimum, reference value or objective formula; a simulator cannot supply certified ground truth
weak: six continuous inputs and no discrete decisions, so the simulator problem goes straight to DFO (last clause of step 7); no surrogate step is mentioned

transferable: Package a simulator-based test problem in four parts: the problem statement, the design variables, a wrapper with a file interface (inputs in one file, objective in another), and instructions that regenerate the target with a pinned simulator version (pp. 2-3).

quotes.text: Given a target rheological behavior and a simulator that predicts rheological behavior from polymer architecture, identify all polymer architectures whose rheological time-behavior resembles that of the target melt.
We recommend using bob version 2.5 for more accurate simulation results.

title: Transfer learning in information criteria-based feature selection
contribution: Embeds Evgeniou-Pontil parameter-sharing transfer learning in Mallows' Cp (TLCp). Under orthogonal design and small task dissimilarity it proves explicit tuning rules under which TLCp selects relevant features more reliably and with lower MSE than Cp, adds asymptotic approximations for correlated designs, and tests on simulations and three real data sets.
problem_entry: Small industrial data sets and transfer-learning error bounds that only make sense for large data: when, and with which tuning, does transfer provably beat independent feature selection at small n (pp. 1-3)?
key_idea: TLCp = shared plus task-specific coefficients with one shared l0 support, eq. (8). It reduces to Cp, to pooled Cp or to sparsity sharing at limiting parameters, and has explicit tuning from Corollary 15 and Theorem 20; for correlated designs, orthogonalize, solve in closed form, back-transform and use Cp-chosen cutoffs (pp. 11-12, 16, 19, 23-26).
assumptions: Linear model, Gaussian noise, orthogonal designs X'X = nI and X~'X~ = mI, sigma-hat ~ sigma; small task dissimilarity delta (kappa bounds) and coefficients away from the critical points; non-orthogonal results are asymptotic in n; the authors call orthogonality the key assumption (pp. 4-5, 11-12, 16, 19-23).
proof_devices: separability under orthogonal design: the l0-penalized least squares splits into k one-dimensional choices between 0 and the OLS value, giving a hard threshold (Proposition 1, p. 7; proof pp. 72-73)
selection probabilities and MSE as Gaussian integrals (Theorems 3 and 6, pp. 7-9); the Cp rule as a z-test at level 2 phi(-sqrt(lambda)/sigma1) (Remark 2, p. 7)
critical-point analysis: a feature with beta^2 = 2 sigma1^2/n is missed with probability 0.5 and a superfluous one kept with probability about 0.16 (Proposition 5 and p. 8)

probability comparison giving tuning conditions (Theorem 12, p. 14), made explicit with a dissimilarity bound kappa (Corollary 15, p. 16); critical-feature probability up to about 0.72 at n = m (Proposition 16, p. 17); MSE dominance (Theorem 20, p. 19)
orthogonalize, solve in closed form, back-transform; consistency in probability (Theorems 23 and 28, pp. 20, 22); percentile cutoffs chosen by the Cp statistic (Theorem 31, p. 23)
experiments: Simulations with known beta (n = m = 20, 5000 data sets per similarity value; correlated features; k up to 30000 at n = m = 30) and three real data sets (blast furnaces, London schools, Parkinson's telemonitoring). Baselines are LASSO, stepwise and univariate selection, their pooled versions and two multi-task methods tuned by 5-fold CV; results carry paired t-tests and CPU time per run; exact Cp and TLCp are solved by enumeration (pp. 29-58; pp. 34, 41).
positioning: Reviews transfer learning with LASSO and SVM without criticism (p. 3). Starts from Mallows' own warning that minimum Cp should not be applied universally (p. 5), and places Cp among AIC, BIC, HQIC and RIC, which ALAMO implements by MIP with BARON (pp. 2, 5).
writing: Each result is followed by a plain-language remark (Remarks 2, 4, 11, 17, 18; pp. 7-18), all proofs go to the appendix (p. 4), and a practitioner's guideline box closes the methods (p. 27).
limits_future: TLCp keeps superfluous features about as often as Cp (pp. 17-18) and may pick wrong models at low similarity (p. 29). Methods coincide above k = 3000 (p. 39). The tuning rules are sub-optimal for correlated designs, so pooled Cp or plain Cp win on some tasks (pp. 45, 51), and no dominance is claimed (p. 57). Exact TLCp is slow (2550.83 s per run, p. 42) and ALAMO is suggested for large k (p. 28). Future work: BIC versions of the delta = 0 results (p. 28).

method_links.note: best-subset selection by an information criterion (Mallows' Cp, l0) in the small-sample regime, framed through ALAMO and BARON and tested against LASSO and other selectors on real data; answers Method 3's small/noisy-data limit by borrowing a related task's data rather than by shrinkage

the exact subset problem is solved by complete enumeration or replaced by a closed-form orthogonalized approximation, not by integer programming; ALAMO only suggested for large k; no first-principles constraints or adaptive sampling

stated tuning protocol for every baseline (5-fold CV over a fixed grid), paired t-tests, CPU time per run, losses and a scope sentence are all reported; but the ground truth is a simulated beta, not a certified optimum, and there is no portfolio conclusion
stand-alone GitHub code; the paper does not say that TLCp went into ALAMO

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the tuning rule of Theorem 20, with estimated variances and dissimilarities, replaces CV and is the stated reason for the speed of the cutoff method; the ALAMO paper sets the fit-complexity trade-off from theory in the same way (card S017, p. 7)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact analysis on the orthogonal design, then orthogonalize and back-transform
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: closed-form hard-threshold solution and exact probabilities under X'X = nI, extended to correlated designs by an invertible Q and back-transformation with asymptotic guarantees

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: computable applicability gate with fallback to the base method
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: transfer only if the relative dissimilarity ||mu_t - mu_s||/||mu_t|| is below 3, otherwise run plain Cp; on a dissimilar Parkinson's task the cutoff method falls back to Cp's performance

transferable: To study an NP-hard l0 criterion, take the orthogonal design first, where it separates into k scalar choices. Compute exact selection probabilities and MSE, locate the failure (critical coefficients missed with probability 0.5), then design the fix for that point and measure it there (pp. 7-8, 17).
Derive hyperparameters from the theorem, plug in estimated variances and dissimilarities, and report CPU time per run against cross-validated baselines (pp. 39-42, 44).
Put a computable gate in front of a transfer method, with an explicit fallback to the base method (p. 27).
End a theory paper with a practitioner's decision box: preprocessing, the gate, and which variant to run when n >= k, when the design is singular, and when n < k (p. 27).
coauthors: Shaohan Chen (first author), Chuanhou Gao (Zhejiang University)

quotes.text: Merely providing tighter upper error bounds is not enough to guarantee that a model selection technique coupled with transfer learning will perform better in real industrial applications with limited data, because these error bounds only make sense in large data size cases.
However, this does not imply that the proposed TLCp methods are always better than the other feature selection methods in any problem.

title: Global Solution of Integer, Stochastic and Nonconvex Optimization Problems
contribution: Guest editors' preface to a Mathematical Programming special issue of 29 papers on exact and provably approximate methods for integer, stochastic and nonconvex problems. It is dedicated to Shabbir Ahmed and states how the editors' own papers were refereed.
problem_entry: n/a as research: the issue is framed by NP-hard problem classes that computational methods nevertheless solve exactly or provably approximately at practical scales (p. 1).
key_idea: n/a as research: Ahmed's work is summarized under three headings, which then sort the 29 papers; the issue's Sahinidis paper is described as quadratic cuts approximating an SDP-equivalent relaxation (pp. 2-5).
positioning: Credits Ahmed with specific firsts (pairing inequalities before multi-row cuts, forbidden vertices, logarithmic piecewise-linear MILP models, SDDIP) and cites two of his papers co-authored with Sahinidis, refs. [9] and [11] (pp. 2-3, 5).
writing: Review-process paragraph: each editor's own paper was handled by another editor (Leyffer for Luedtke's, Luedtke for Sahinidis's), and neither editor had any information about his paper's review (p. 5).

method_links.note: weak: the three editors summarize the issue's Nohra-Raghunathan-Sahinidis paper as convex quadratic cuts that outer-approximate a semi-infinite convex relaxation equivalent, under conditions, to a well-known SDP relaxation (step 3); SKILL.md already cites the paper

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: editor's own paper handled by a co-editor, blind to its review
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Sahinidis's co-authored paper in his own guest-edited issue was handled by co-editor Luedtke, and he had no information about its review; one instance, bearing on the skill's gap about referees

transferable: When editing a special issue or proceedings, say in the preface who handled the editors' own submissions, and that the editors saw nothing of those reviews (p. 5).
Sort the papers of a collection under the same headings used to summarize the founding work, so that each paper is placed against it (pp. 2-5).
coauthors: Santanu S. Dey, James R. Luedtke

quotes.text: Despite this challenge, there has been tremendous advances in computational methods that can provide exact or provably approximate solutions to these problems at scales of practical interest.
Neither Luedtke nor Sahinidis had any information about the review of their papers.

title: Optimizing the designs and operations of water networks: A decomposition approach
contribution: Conference talk, an early version of S165, that models produced-water network design and operation jointly and supplies SCIP with incumbents from a CVXNLP-based or a time decomposition. The gaps close to at most 13.53% where SCIP alone finds no feasible point.
problem_entry: Produced-water networks need design (pipe sizes, pumps) and operation (flows, pressures) in one multi-period model; BARON and SCIP improve dual bounds but are slow to find feasible points (pp. 3, 7, 17).
key_idea: Two primal heuristics hand an incumbent to SCIP: a budget loop with a CVXNLP-based master, a fixed-diameter feasibility subproblem and no-good cuts; and a time decomposition that solves the first T~ periods to gap epsilon, fixes the design and checks the rest (pp. 18-30).
assumptions: Directed graph, diameter choices, relief valves, at most N pumps with min-up/min-down and an operation cap; Hazen-Williams pressure drop; objective = diameter cost; CVXNLP needs a strictly increasing pressure-drop function with phi(0) = 0; the time decomposition relies on falling volumes (pp. 8-15, 20, 25).
proof_devices: cited equivalence theorem (c.f. Raghunathan 2013; CVXNLP after Cherry 1951): the network analysis equations are solvable iff CVXNLP is, so a convex program replaces the nonconvex pressure equations in the master (pp. 19-20)
integer no-good cuts on infeasible subproblems (p. 24)
experiments: One PARETO case (19 sources, 7 sinks, 29 in-nodes, 58 pipes; 4 diameters; 53 periods) at five stress factors. SCIP alone finds no primal solution; the time decomposition ends at gaps of 0.00-13.53%; the CVXNLP route reaches up to 94.77% and fails at stress 2.0; SCIP alone keeps slightly higher dual bounds (pp. 30-32).
positioning: Prior design and operation papers (Bragalli et al. 2012, Raghunathan 2013, Rajagopalan 2018, Pecci et al. 2019, Ghaddar et al. 2015, Bonvin et al. 2021) are restated without criticism under separate headings (pp. 4-6).
writing: Deck order: application, previous works, model, challenges, two primal methods, experiments, summary; one slide names the primal side as the bottleneck (pp. 3-33).
limits_future: CVXNLP struggles as stress grows; the restricted problem can itself be hard for SCIP, so combining the two methods is suggested; no code or data release is mentioned (pp. 32-34).

method_links.note: step 2 (good incumbent early): the primal side is named as the bottleneck and an incumbent is supplied from outside; the reason given is feasibility, not reduction, and the hand-off does not raise SCIP's dual bound; same diagnosis as the journal version S165
all problems are solved by SCIP; BARON is named only as able to handle the constraints; the methods live outside any solver
one PARETO case with stress-factor scenarios, no public library and no certified optimum; gaps are measured against SCIP's dual bound

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: decompose for the incumbent, let the general solver bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: problem-specific decompositions only supply the primal solution, and SCIP keeps the full model and the dual bound; same project as S165, not independent
solve the high-volume early periods to a target gap, fix the design and pump locations, check the remaining periods, scan T~ and epsilon; same project as S165

transferable: When a general solver bounds well but finds no feasible point, write a problem-specific decomposition whose only job is an incumbent, and hand that over as a starting point. Report solver-alone against heuristic-then-solver with primal, dual and gap per scenario (pp. 17, 30, 32).
Justify a time decomposition by the physics of the instance (falling volumes), then scan the split period and the target gap over small sets (pp. 25-29).
coauthors: Yijiang Li (first author), Santanu Dey, Naresh Susarla, Miguel Zamarripa-Perez, Markus Drouven

quotes.text: Solvers like BARON and SCIP can improve on the dual bounds, but can be slow in obtaining primal (feasible) solutions
It can be difficult to solve even the restricted problem directly by SCIP; opportunity to combined the two methods

title: Announcement: Howard Rosenbrock Prize 2022
contribution: Editorial notice of the 2022 Rosenbrock Prize to Subramanyam for a Lagrangian dual method in two-stage robust optimization with binary uncertainties. The citation comes from a committee that included Sahinidis and praises a generic method that beats domain-specific ones.
key_idea: n/a: same template as S294 (winner, committee, quoted citation, previous winners, invitation) (pp. 1-2)
positioning: The committee (Raghunathan, Ploskas, Sahinidis) praises an exact, generic method that plugs into existing algorithms and is much faster than domain-specific approaches on network design, facility location and staff rostering (p. 1).
writing: The citation's closing sentence on theoretical and practical relevance repeats the 2021 committee's sentence nearly word for word, with the problem class swapped (p. 1; S294 pp. 1-2).

quotes.text: The other committee members were Nikolaos Ploskas (University of Western Macedonia, Greece) and Nick Sahinidis (Georgia Institute of Technology, USA).

The numerical experiments on a variety of problems (network design, facility location, and staff rostering) demonstrate that the generic approach developed in the paper shows significant computational speedups over the existing, domain-specific approaches.
